translations.answer: HumanUP first discovers getting-up trajectories under broad collision and pose randomization, then trains a tracking policy against slowed references. The paper reports bounded G1 hardware results across six surfaces, with failures on slopes and snow, so it is a recovery method with explicit state and terrain limits rather than a guarantee for every fall.
translations.applicability.assumptions.0: The fallen state lies within the training randomization support and perception and actuators remain available.
translations.applicability.assumptions.1: Hardware testing uses an independent emergency stop, limits, a padded area, and staged progression.
translations.applicability.controllers.0: Reinforcement-learning discovery policy and slowed-trajectory tracking policy.
translations.applicability.environments.0: The six surfaces and controlled hardware trials reported in the paper.
translations.confidence_rationale: The paper reports simulation ablations and hardware success rates on six surfaces. Slope and snow failures, limited trial counts, and robot-specific safety requirements bound extrapolation.
translations.evidence.0.locator: Figures 2–8, Tables I–III, Sections III–IV, and the appendix.
translations.evidence.0.note: Defines two-stage discovery/tracking, randomization, and curricula, and reports simulation and six-surface hardware results.
translations.evidence.0.title: Learning Getting-Up Policies for Real-World Humanoid Robots
translations.title: Has HumanUP solved hardware getting-up for arbitrary terrains and fallen poses?
